speaker: Mike Krieger
title: Anthropic's CPO on what comes next | Mike Krieger
question: In AI products, why do traditional consumer engagement metrics often mislead product teams?
guest: It would be very dangerous to over-optimize on likability, because you can fall into making the AI sycophantic, telling you what you want to hear, or prolonging conversations just for the sake of prolonging them. At Instagram, time spent was the metric we looked at a lot, and we evolved it toward healthy time spent, but overall that was the north star. That would be the wrong approach here. It is not the Web 2.0 or social media engagement metrics—it should really be around whether the AI actually helped you get your work done. For example, Claude helped me build a prototype that saved me roughly six hours in about 20 minutes. That is much harder to quantify on a dashboard without annoying surveys. Often teams get overly metrics-obsessed when they are trying to convince themselves a product is serving people when it is not. The north star should be whether people repeatedly unlock creativity, get things done, and gain more space in their lives.

points.core: Optimizing AI products for likability incentivizes sycophantic responses that agree with users.
points.note: Accept: optimizing thumbs-up or likability causing flattery, yes-man behavior, or telling users what they want to hear instead of truthful answers. Do not credit: generic claims about AI bias or hallucinations.

points.core: Optimizing for time spent pushes models to artificially prolong conversations unnecessarily.
points.note: Accept: session-length or message-count targets rewarding drawn-out back-and-forth instead of fast problem resolution. Do not credit: generic criticism of vanity metrics without tying to prolonged AI chats.

points.core: Effective AI products often shrink session duration by saving users hours of work.
points.note: Accept: real AI value manifesting as completed tasks or major time savings even in brief interactions, which engagement dashboards misread as low usage. Do not credit: generic advice to focus on user value.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Traditional engagement metrics were built for products where more time and more clicks signal more value, such as feeds, games, and social apps. AI products usually invert that logic: their value lies in getting a task done quickly and correctly, so the usual signals become ambiguous or even backwards.

A long session or a high message count may mean the user is delighted, or that the model kept failing and they had to rephrase, retry, and correct it. A short session may mean the answer was right first time. Likewise, daily active use can reflect novelty or curiosity rather than durable value, and retention can look healthy while users quietly distrust the outputs and verify everything elsewhere.

These metrics also miss quality. They do not capture whether the answer was accurate, whether the user accepted or heavily edited it, or whether it actually saved time. Optimising for them can push teams toward verbosity, flattery, or stickiness rather than usefulness.

Better signals are outcome-based: task success rate, time to a usable result, acceptance and edit rates, regeneration frequency, and repeat use for the same job.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Traditional consumer engagement metrics—such as time spent, session length, and interaction frequency—assume that more activity equals more value. In AI products, that relationship is often inverted. Because most AI tools exist to resolve tasks rather than capture attention, a long session with many back-and-forth turns frequently signals friction: the model misunderstood intent, hallucinated, or forced the user into frustrating prompt retries. Conversely, a single-turn interaction lasting seconds often represents a perfect outcome.

These metrics also blind teams to the unique economics and usage patterns of AI. Unlike conventional software with near-zero marginal costs, every extra turn consumes expensive inference compute, meaning bloated engagement from repeated retries simultaneously erodes user trust and gross margins. At the same time, novelty-driven curiosity ("AI tourism") can temporarily inflate active-user counts without reflecting durable utility, while agentic features increasingly execute work asynchronously in the background with almost no UI interaction at all. Consequently, teams that optimize for clicks or screen time risk rewarding model failure instead of measuring true task completion and retained value.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Traditional engagement metrics like time-in-app, session counts and daily active users assume that more use means more value. That assumption often fails for AI products. A good AI assistant is supposed to save time, so when it solves a problem in one exchange, sessions get shorter. When it fails, users rephrase, retry and correct it, and that frustration shows up as "engagement." Long conversations can mean confusion rather than delight.

Usage also can't separate real value from novelty. Many AI products see big early spikes from curiosity that fade once the newness wears off, which hides weak retention. Raw usage also says nothing about whether outputs were correct, trusted or actually used. A user might copy a hallucinated answer, or quietly redo the work by hand.

Optimizing for engagement can push teams toward bad incentives too: chattier responses, sycophancy, or companion-style designs that encourage compulsive use instead of solving problems.

Better signals focus on outcomes. These include task completion, how often outputs are accepted or kept versus edited or regenerated, time-to-resolution, and whether users come back for new tasks rather than retries. Long-term cohort retention, user willingness to pay, and quality evaluations tied to real user intent also help.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Traditional consumer engagement metrics, such as session length, time on site, and interaction counts, were built for attention-driven products where more activity reliably signals more value. In AI products, that relationship often inverts. A long conversation with many turns frequently indicates friction rather than delight: the model misunderstood the user, produced an inaccurate or generic output, or forced repeated prompt refinements. Conversely, when an AI feature works exceptionally well, it resolves the user's need in a single turn, shrinking session duration and making great performance look like declining engagement.

Raw activity metrics also obscure the gap between novelty and lasting utility, since users often generate high early volume just experimenting without adopting the tool into real workflows. Worse, optimizing for engagement can actively degrade the product by rewarding chatty or sycophantic responses over concise, accurate ones. Outcome-oriented signals—like task completion, output acceptance, and edit rates—measure real value far better.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Traditional engagement metrics tell you how much people use an AI product. The same numbers can rise when the product helps and when it fails. More messages or longer sessions might reflect productive collaboration, or they might mean users keep rephrasing prompts and correcting mistakes. A user who gets a reliable answer in one turn may leave quickly because the product did exactly what they needed. Even retention depends on how often the underlying task comes up.

Teams get a clearer picture by pairing engagement with task outcomes. Did users finish the job? Was the result accurate and usable? How much time, effort, and rework did it take? Engagement is easier to interpret once you know what users accomplished.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Traditional engagement metrics often assume that more time, clicks, or return visits mean the product is delivering more value. In an AI product, the same behavior can signal either success or friction. A user might spend 20 minutes refining a draft because the collaboration is valuable, or because the model keeps missing the point. Another user might get exactly what they need on the first try and leave.

The risk is that a team optimizing for engagement rewards extra work for the user. Engagement is easier to interpret alongside measures tied to the user’s goal, such as whether they completed the task, how well the result met their needs, and how much effort it took.
